title: Biological Molecules
seo_title: Secondary 3 Biology: Biological Molecules Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_text: State the roles of water in living organisms; describe the structure of carbohydrates, fats and proteins in terms of their smaller basic units, and condensation and hydrolysis; describe and carry out tests for starch, reducing sugars, protein and fats; explain enzyme action using the lock-and-key hypothesis, and investigate and explain the effects of temperature and pH on enzyme activity (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Biology worksheets on biological molecules: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, food tests, Benedict's test, enzymes, temperature and pH. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Big molecules are chains of small units.
key_sub: Enzymes are proteins: specific, and denatured by heat or extreme pH.
body_html:
How to think about it

Know the units and the tests.

  • Starch, glycogen and cellulose: many glucose. Fats: glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Proteins: amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
  • Condensation joins units (water removed); hydrolysis breaks them (water added).
  • Iodine: blue-black (starch). Benedict's, heated: blue → brick-red (reducing sugar). Biuret: violet (protein). Ethanol: cloudy emulsion (fat).
  • Enzymes have an active site that fits one substrate. Activity rises to an optimum temperature, then falls as the enzyme is denatured.
Example

6 glucose join to make a chain. Water molecules?

5 bonds form

one water per bond

Answer: 5

Example

Biuret turns violet. Present?

biuret tests protein

Answer: protein

Common mistakes

  • Saying enzymes are “killed” by heat.
  • Saying sucrose is a reducing sugar.
  • Mixing up glycogen (animals) and starch (plants).
  • Saying a positive Benedict's test stays blue.

faq.q: What is the difference between starch, glycogen and cellulose?
faq.a: All are polysaccharides of glucose. Starch is the storage carbohydrate in plants, glycogen in animals, and cellulose forms plant cell walls.

faq.q: Why do enzymes stop working at high temperatures?
faq.a: Above the optimum temperature the enzyme is denatured: the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits.

faq.q: How do you test for a reducing sugar?
faq.a: Add Benedict's solution and heat in a boiling water bath. A green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitate shows a reducing sugar.

items.q: Why are biological washing powders less effective in very hot water?

items.q: An enzyme's activity falls sharply above 45 °C and does not recover when cooled. Why?
c: The enzyme is denatured: the shape of its active site has changed permanently.
items.e: Enzymes are proteins, not living things.

items.q: Cellulose and starch are both made of glucose. Why can humans not digest cellulose?

Cellulose is not made of glucose.
items.e: Cellulose is dietary fibre.

items.q: Why does pepsin work in the stomach but not in the small intestine?
c: Pepsin is used up in the stomach.
There is no protein in the small intestine.
The small intestine is too cold.
Its optimum pH is about 2; the small intestine is alkaline.
items.e: Each enzyme has an optimum pH.
